note: First-reading proposals the second reading judged unnecessary (the current English is an acceptable rendering of the Latin). Kept for the record; no change proposed.

withdrawn.latin: Ligans ad vineam pullum suum, et ad vitem, o fili mi, asinam suam, lavabit in vino stolam suam et in sanguine uvæ pallium suum.
withdrawn.english: Binding his colt to the vine, and his female donkey to the vine, O my son, he shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape.

first_reading.proposed: Binding his colt to the vineyard, and his female donkey to the vine, O my son, he shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape.
first_reading.reason: "ad vineam" is "to the vineyard"; only "ad vitem" is "to the vine". The English renders both nouns as "vine", losing the Latin's distinction.

second_reading.note: "vinea" also means a vine in Vulgate usage (Ezek 17:6), and a colt is tied to a vine; "ad vineam ... ad vitem" as vine twice is defensible.

withdrawn.latin: quorum Nadab et Abiu mortui sunt, cum obtulissent ignem alienum coram Domino.
withdrawn.english: Of these, Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the Lord.

first_reading.proposed: Of these, Nadab and Abihu died when they offered strange fire before the Lord.
first_reading.reason: "ignem alienum" is strange/foreign fire; "unauthorized" is an interpretation the word alienus does not carry.

second_reading.note: 'ignem alienum': alienus covers what is foreign or improper to the rite (Lev 10:1 'quod eis praeceptum non erat'), so 'unauthorized' is a legitimate rendering.

withdrawn.latin: Et ligabis ea quasi signum in manu tua, eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos,
withdrawn.english: Bind them as a sign on your hand; they shall hang and move between your eyes.

first_reading.proposed: Bind them as a sign on your hand; they shall be and shall move between your eyes.
first_reading.reason: "eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos": they shall be and shall move between your eyes; "hang" is not what "erunt" says.

second_reading.note: 'eruntque et movebuntur inter oculos tuos': 'hang' is an idiomatic English verb for locative 'erunt' beside 'movebuntur'; sense is unchanged.

withdrawn.latin: Non miseraberis ejus, et auferes innoxium sanguinem de Israël, ut bene sit tibi.
withdrawn.english: Do not pity him. Remove the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may go well with you.

first_reading.proposed: Do not pity him. Remove the innocent blood from Israel, so that it may go well with you.
first_reading.reason: "auferes innoxium sanguinem de Israël": you shall take away the innocent blood; "the guilt of" is an interpretive addition not in the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'auferes innoxium sanguinem': blood stands for bloodguilt; 'the guilt of' only spells out that metonymy, as Douay also does, without changing the sense.

withdrawn.latin: Legem præcepit nobis Moyses, hæreditatem multitudinis Jacob.
withdrawn.english: Moses commanded us a law, the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob.

first_reading.proposed: Moses commanded us a law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob.
first_reading.reason: 'haereditatem multitudinis Jacob' = the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob; 'assembly' is not a sense of 'multitudo' and reflects the Hebrew/KJV 'congregation'.

second_reading.note: 'multitudinis Jacob': in the Vulgate multitudo regularly denotes the whole body or community of the people, so 'assembly' is within its range.

withdrawn.latin: et tulit baculum suum, quem semper habebat in manibus : et elegit sibi quinque limpidissimos lapides de torrente, et misit eos in peram pastoralem quam habebat secum, et fundam manu tulit : et processit adversum Philisthæum.
withdrawn.english: and took his staff, which he always carried in his hands. He chose five very smooth stones from the torrent bed and put them in the shepherd's bag he had with him. He took his sling in his hand and went toward the Philistine.

first_reading.proposed: and took his staff, which he always carried in his hands. He chose five very clear stones from the torrent bed and put them in the shepherd's bag he had with him. He took his sling in his hand and went toward the Philistine.
first_reading.reason: Latin 'limpidissimos lapides' = 'very clear/bright stones'; 'very smooth' is the Hebrew's word (kept by Douay), not a sense of 'limpidus'.

second_reading.note: 'limpidissimos lapides': of brook stones limpidus means bright, polished; 'very smooth' is the accepted rendering (Douay), and proposed 'clear stones' misleads.

withdrawn.latin: Dedisti mihi clypeum salutis tuæ, et mansuetudo tua multiplicavit me.
withdrawn.english: You gave me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness made me great.

first_reading.proposed: You gave me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness multiplied me.
first_reading.reason: "multiplicavit me" means multiplied/increased me; "made me great" is the KJV/Hebrew wording rather than this Latin verb.

second_reading.note: 'mansuetudo tua multiplicavit me': multiplicare also means increase, enlarge, so 'made me great' is within range; 'multiplied me' is poorer English.

withdrawn.latin: Cumque ascendissent viri Israël, ipse stetit et percussit Philisthæos donec deficeret manus ejus, et obrigesceret cum gladio : fecitque Dominus salutem magnam in die illa : et populus qui fugerat, reversus est ad cæsorum spolia detrahenda.
withdrawn.english: When the men of Israel had withdrawn, he stood and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stiffened around the sword. The Lord brought about a great deliverance that day, and the people who had fled returned to strip the slain of their spoils.

first_reading.proposed: When the men of Israel had gone up, he stood and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stiffened around the sword. The Lord brought about a great deliverance that day, and the people who had fled returned to strip the slain of their spoils.
first_reading.reason: "Cumque ascendissent viri Israël" says the men of Israel had gone up; "had withdrawn" is an interpretation not in the verb ascendere.

second_reading.note: 'Cumque ascendissent viri Israel': with 'populus qui fugerat' following, the going up is a departure (Douay 'were gone away'); 'withdrawn' is a sound contextual rendering.

withdrawn.latin: Abialbon Arbathites, Azmaveth de Beromi,
withdrawn.english: Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth of Bahurim;

first_reading.proposed: Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth the Barhumite;
first_reading.reason: "Azmaveth de Beromi" (the Barhumite) is rendered "of Bahurim", a different name which the Vulgate spells Bahurim elsewhere; the identification is an inference, not the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'Azmaveth de Beromi' is 'of' a place; 'of Bahurim' is the standard modern form for it, while proposed 'the Barhumite' swaps the Latin 'de' for a KJV gentilic.

withdrawn.latin: Ambulavitque in omni via Jeroboam filii Nabat, et in peccatis ejus quibus peccare fecerat Israël, ut irritaret Dominum Deum Israël in vanitatibus suis.
withdrawn.english: He walked in every way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in the sins by which he had caused Israel to sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, with their vanities.

first_reading.proposed: He walked in every way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in the sins by which he had caused Israel to sin, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, with his vanities.
first_reading.reason: 'ut irritaret... in vanitatibus suis': the verb is singular (Omri), so reflexive 'suis' is 'his vanities'; 'their vanities' follows the Hebrew/Douay plural.

second_reading.note: 'in vanitatibus suis': Vulgate 'suus' is often loosely used and can refer to 'Israel' just named; Douay also reads 'their vanities', so the current English is defensible.

withdrawn.latin: Ego dormivi, et soporatus sum ; et exsurrexi, quia Dominus suscepit me.
withdrawn.english: I lay down and slept, and I arose, for the Lord sustained me.

first_reading.proposed: I slept and was fast asleep, and I arose, for the Lord sustained me.
first_reading.reason: "Ego dormivi, et soporatus sum" = I slept and was sunk in sleep; "I lay down and slept" follows the Hebrew wording, not dormivi / soporatus sum.

second_reading.note: "dormivi, et soporatus sum": Vulgate dormire covers lying down to sleep and soporatus the sleep itself; current is sound and the proposal is tautological.

withdrawn.latin: Specie tua et pulchritudine tua intende, prospere procede, et regna, propter veritatem, et mansuetudinem, et justitiam ; et deducet te mirabiliter dextera tua.
withdrawn.english: In your splendor and your beauty draw your bow, advance prosperously, and reign for the sake of truth, gentleness, and righteousness; your right hand will guide you wonderfully.

first_reading.proposed: In your splendor and your beauty set out, advance prosperously, and reign for the sake of truth, gentleness, and righteousness; your right hand will guide you wonderfully.
first_reading.reason: "intende" stands alone (set out, press on); the Latin has no "arcum". "draw your bow" supplies an object the Latin lacks.

second_reading.note: "intende": intendere (arcum) is the standard verb for bending a bow, and arrows follow; a legitimate reading, no worse than "set out".

withdrawn.latin: quia comederunt Jacob, et locum ejus desolaverunt.
withdrawn.english: because they have devoured Jacob and laid his dwelling waste.

first_reading.proposed: because they have devoured Jacob and laid his place waste.
first_reading.reason: "locum ejus" is "his place"; "dwelling" reflects the Hebrew/KJV "dwelling place", not the Latin word.

second_reading.note: 'locum ejus' is the place where Jacob lives; 'his dwelling' is a sound contextual rendering of locus and changes nothing asserted.

withdrawn.latin: bestiæ, et universa pecora ; serpentes, et volucres pennatæ ;
withdrawn.english: wild beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds;

first_reading.proposed: wild beasts and all cattle, serpents and winged birds;
first_reading.reason: "serpentes" is "serpents"; "creeping things" is the Hebrew/KJV wording, not the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'serpentes' is the participle of serpere used as a noun, 'creeping things' as well as 'serpents'; the current English is within its range.

withdrawn.latin: Cogitationes justorum judicia, et consilia impiorum fraudulenta.
withdrawn.english: The thoughts of the just are right judgments, and the counsels of the wicked are deceitful.

first_reading.proposed: The thoughts of the just are judgments, and the counsels of the wicked are deceitful.
first_reading.reason: Latin "Cogitationes justorum judicia" has only "judgments"; "right" is added (cf. KJV "are right"), with no Latin word behind it.

second_reading.note: 'judicia' set against 'fraudulenta' carries the biblical sense of what is just; 'right judgments' unpacks that one word rather than adding a new idea.

withdrawn.latin: Ex ipsis exaltavit et magnificavit Deus, et ex ipsis posuit in numerum dierum : et omnes homines de solo et ex terra unde creatus est Adam.
withdrawn.english: Some of them God exalted and magnified, and some He placed among the ordinary days. All human beings are from the soil and from the earth from which Adam was created.

first_reading.proposed: Some of them God exalted and magnified, and some He placed in the number of days. All human beings are from the soil and from the earth from which Adam was created.
first_reading.reason: Latin 'posuit in numerum dierum' is 'placed in the number of days'; 'ordinary' is an interpretive addition with no Latin word behind it.

second_reading.note: 'posuit in numerum dierum', set against 'exaltavit et magnificavit', means the common run of days; Douay reads it the same way, so 'ordinary days' is faithful.

withdrawn.latin: quia factus es fortitudo pauperi, fortitudo egeno in tribulatione sua, spes a turbine, umbraculum ab æstu ; spiritus enim robustorum quasi turbo impellens parietem.
withdrawn.english: because You have become strength for the poor, strength for the needy in their distress, a refuge from the whirlwind, shade from the heat; for the breath of the mighty is like a whirlwind beating against a wall.

first_reading.proposed: because You have become strength for the poor, strength for the needy in their distress, a hope from the whirlwind, shade from the heat; for the breath of the mighty is like a whirlwind beating against a wall.
first_reading.reason: "spes a turbine": spes is hope; "refuge" reflects the Hebrew word behind it (and the Douay wording), not the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'spes a turbine', hope as protection from the whirlwind, is idiomatically 'refuge', as Douay also reads; 'a hope from the whirlwind' is poorer English with no gain.

withdrawn.latin: ut sugatis et repleamini ab ubere consolationis ejus ; ut mulgeatis et deliciis affluatis ab omnimoda gloria ejus.
withdrawn.english: so that you may suck and be filled from her consoling breast, draw milk, and overflow with delights from the abundance of her glory.

first_reading.proposed: so that you may suck and be filled from her consoling breast, draw milk, and overflow with delights from her glory of every kind.
first_reading.reason: 'ab omnimoda gloria ejus' is 'from her glory of every kind'; 'abundance of her glory' is the Hebrew/KJV phrase, not the sense of omnimodus.

second_reading.note: 'ab omnimoda gloria ejus' (glory of every kind) is fairly paraphrased as 'abundance of her glory', as Douay also reads; the difference is stylistic.

withdrawn.latin: Filii colligunt ligna, et patres succendunt ignem, et mulieres conspergunt adipem, ut faciant placentas reginæ cæli, et libent diis alienis, et me ad iracundiam provocent.
withdrawn.english: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead the rich dough to make cakes for the queen of heaven, to pour out offerings to foreign gods and provoke Me to anger.

first_reading.proposed: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women sprinkle the fat to make cakes for the queen of heaven, to pour out offerings to foreign gods and provoke Me to anger.
first_reading.reason: "mulieres conspergunt adipem" = 'the women sprinkle the fat'; 'knead the rich dough' follows the Hebrew, not the Latin.

second_reading.note: In Vulgate usage 'conspergere' is to moisten or knead meal (cf. conspersio, dough) and 'adeps' the rich flour; 'sprinkle the fat' would misrender 'conspergunt adipem'.

withdrawn.latin: Ecce enim dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, et convertam conversionem populi mei Israël et Juda, ait Dominus : et convertam eos ad terram quam dedi patribus eorum, et possidebunt eam.
withdrawn.english: For behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will restore the fortunes of My people Israel and Judah, says the Lord. I will bring them back to the land I gave their fathers, and they will possess it.”

first_reading.proposed: For behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will bring about the return of My people Israel and Judah, says the Lord. I will bring them back to the land I gave their fathers, and they will possess it.”
first_reading.reason: 'convertam conversionem' is 'I will turn the turning/bring back the return (captivity)'; 'restore the fortunes' is the modern rendering of the Hebrew idiom, not of Latin 'conversionem'.

second_reading.note: 'convertam conversionem' is an opaque calque (turn the turning); 'restore the fortunes' is a fair idiomatic rendering, and 'bring about the return' is no closer.

withdrawn.latin: Hæc dicit Dominus : Ecce ego convertam conversionem tabernaculorum Jacob, et tectis ejus miserebor : et ædificabitur civitas in excelso suo, et templum juxta ordinem suum fundabitur :
withdrawn.english: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will restore the fortunes of Jacob’s tents and have mercy on his dwellings. The city will be built upon its height, and the temple will be established according to its order.

first_reading.proposed: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring about the return of Jacob’s tents and have mercy on his dwellings. The city will be built upon its height, and the temple will be established according to its order.
first_reading.reason: 'convertam conversionem tabernaculorum Jacob' is 'I will bring back the return (captivity) of Jacob's tents'; 'restore the fortunes' follows the modern reading of the Hebrew, not Latin 'conversionem'.

second_reading.note: 'convertam conversionem tabernaculorum Jacob' is the same calque; 'restore the fortunes' is fair idiom, and 'the return of Jacob's tents' is no more exact.

withdrawn.latin: Et convertam conversionem Juda et conversionem Jerusalem, et ædificabo eos sicut a principio.
withdrawn.english: I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Jerusalem and rebuild them as at the beginning.

first_reading.proposed: I will bring about the return of Judah and the return of Jerusalem and rebuild them as at the beginning.
first_reading.reason: 'convertam conversionem Juda et conversionem Jerusalem' is 'I will bring back the return (captivity) of Judah and of Jerusalem'; 'restore the fortunes' is the modern reading of the Hebrew, not Latin 'conversionem'.

second_reading.note: 'convertam conversionem Juda et conversionem Jerusalem' is the same calque; 'restore the fortunes' is an acceptable idiomatic rendering of it.

withdrawn.latin: vox gaudii et vox lætitiæ, vox sponsi et vox sponsæ, vox dicentium : Confitemini Domino exercituum, quoniam bonus Dominus, quoniam in æternum misericordia ejus : et portantium vota in domum Domini : reducam enim conversionem terræ sicut a principio, dicit Dominus.
withdrawn.english: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who say, ‘Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for His mercy endures forever,’ and of those who bring vowed offerings to the house of the Lord. For I will restore the fortunes of the land as at the beginning, says the Lord.

first_reading.proposed: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who say, ‘Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for His mercy endures forever,’ and of those who bring vowed offerings to the house of the Lord. For I will bring back the return of the land as at the beginning, says the Lord.
first_reading.reason: 'reducam conversionem terræ' is 'I will bring back the return (captivity) of the land'; 'restore the fortunes' renders the modern reading of the Hebrew, not Latin 'conversionem'.

second_reading.note: 'reducam conversionem terræ' is the same calque; 'restore the fortunes of the land' is fair idiom, and 'bring back the return' is no clearer or closer.

withdrawn.latin: Et confortabo brachia regis Babylonis, daboque gladium meum in manu ejus, et confringam brachia Pharaonis, et gement gemitibus interfecti coram facie ejus.
withdrawn.english: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put My sword in his hand. I will break Pharaoh's arms, and they will groan before him with the groans of the slain.

first_reading.proposed: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put My sword in his hand. I will break Pharaoh's arms, and the slain will groan with groanings before him.
first_reading.reason: "gement gemitibus interfecti": "interfecti" is nominative, the subject (the slain will groan with groans); "with the groans of the slain" is the Hebrew construction, not the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'interfecti' can equally be genitive singular with 'gemitibus' (groans of a slain man), which the current renders; the nominative parse is not required.

withdrawn.latin: [Hæc dicit Dominus Deus : In die illa, ascendent sermones super cor tuum, et cogitabis cogitationem pessimam :
withdrawn.english: Thus says the Lord God: On that day thoughts will rise in your heart, and you will devise a most evil plan.

first_reading.proposed: Thus says the Lord God: On that day words will rise in your heart, and you will devise a most evil plan.
first_reading.reason: Latin 'ascendent sermones super cor tuum': 'sermones' are words, not 'thoughts' (the modern rendering of the Hebrew).

second_reading.note: 'ascendent sermones super cor tuum': words rising upon the heart are idiomatically thoughts; Douay likewise paraphrases ('projects'). Acceptable idiom.

withdrawn.latin: Qui fabricati sunt limen suum juxta limen meum, et postes suos juxta postes meos, et murus erat inter me et eos : et polluerunt nomen sanctum meum in abominationibus quas fecerunt : propter quod consumpsi eos in ira mea.
withdrawn.english: They built their threshold beside My threshold and their doorposts beside My doorposts, with only a wall between Me and them. They profaned My holy name by the abominations they committed; therefore I consumed them in My anger.

first_reading.proposed: They built their threshold beside My threshold and their doorposts beside My doorposts, and there was a wall between Me and them. They profaned My holy name by the abominations they committed; therefore I consumed them in My anger.
first_reading.reason: 'et murus erat inter me et eos' says 'and there was a wall between me and them'; 'only' is added and is not in the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'et murus erat inter me et eos': 'only' brings out the implied point of the complaint, as Douay's 'but a wall' also does; acceptable idiom.

withdrawn.latin: Deus meus misit angelum suum, et conclusit ora leonum, et non nocuerunt mihi : quia coram eo justitia inventa est in me : sed et coram te, rex, delictum non feci.
withdrawn.english: My God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not harmed me, because innocence was found in me before Him. Nor have I committed any offense against you, O king.”

first_reading.proposed: My God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not harmed me, because justice was found in me before Him. Nor have I committed any offense against you, O king.”
first_reading.reason: 'justitia inventa est in me' is 'justice (righteousness) was found in me'; 'innocence' follows the Aramaic rather than the Latin 'justitia'.

second_reading.note: 'justitia inventa est in me' in this forensic setting is being found in the right; 'innocence' lies within that sense.

withdrawn.latin: Et dixit Aggæus : Si tetigerit pollutus in anima ex omnibus his, numquid contaminabitur ? Et responderunt sacerdotes, et dixerunt : Contaminabitur.
withdrawn.english: Then Haggai said, “If someone made unclean by a dead body touches any of these things, will it become unclean?” The priests answered, “It will become unclean.”

first_reading.proposed: Then Haggai said, “If someone made unclean by a soul touches any of these things, will it become unclean?” The priests answered, “It will become unclean.”
first_reading.reason: Latin has 'pollutus in anima' (defiled by/in a soul); 'by a dead body' substitutes the sense of the Hebrew term for the Latin word 'anima'.

second_reading.note: 'pollutus in anima' uses 'anima' in the Vulgate's sense of a (dead) person; 'by a dead body' renders that, while 'by a soul' is obscure English.

withdrawn.latin: Et dicetur ei : Quid sunt plagæ istæ in medio manuum tuarum ? Et dicet : His plagatus sum in domo eorum qui diligebant me.]
withdrawn.english: He will be asked, “What are these wounds between your hands?” He will say, “I was wounded with these in the house of those who loved me.”

first_reading.proposed: He will be asked, “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” He will say, “I was wounded with these in the house of those who loved me.”
first_reading.reason: "in medio manuum tuarum" = in the midst (middle) of your hands; "between your hands" is the Hebrew idiom and moves the wounds off the hands.

second_reading.note: 'in medio' with a genitive plural regularly means between/among; 'between your hands' is within the range of 'in medio manuum tuarum'.

withdrawn.latin: Præ timore autem ejus exterriti sunt custodes, et facti sunt velut mortui.
withdrawn.english: The guards were shaken with fear of him and became like dead men.

first_reading.proposed: The guards were struck with terror for fear of him and became like dead men.
first_reading.reason: "were shaken" renders the Greek verb (shook); the Latin "exterriti sunt" means were terrified, struck with terror, with no idea of shaking.

second_reading.note: 'præ timore … exterriti sunt' is struck with terror from fear; 'shaken with fear' is an acceptable English idiom for the same state.

withdrawn.latin: hic erit magnus, et Filius Altissimi vocabitur, et dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus: et regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum,
withdrawn.english: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever,

first_reading.proposed: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob forever,
first_reading.reason: 'regnabit in domo Jacob' is 'will reign in the house of Jacob'; 'over' reflects the Greek preposition rather than the Latin 'in'.

second_reading.note: 'regnabit in domo Jacob': reigning in the house as its king is reigning over it; the preposition makes no difference of sense.

withdrawn.latin: Venit autem et Nicodemus, qui venerat ad Jesum nocte primum, ferens mixturam myrrhæ et aloës, quasi libras centum.
withdrawn.english: Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds.

first_reading.proposed: Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.
first_reading.reason: "quasi libras centum" = about a hundred pounds; "Roman" is an explanatory addition not in the Latin.

second_reading.note: 'libras centum': the libra is the Roman pound, so 'Roman pounds' is an accurate rendering of the unit, not a departure.

withdrawn.latin: Ideo habentes administrationem, juxta quod misericordiam consecuti sumus, non deficimus,
withdrawn.english: Therefore seeing we have this ministration, just as we have obtained mercy, we faint not.

first_reading.proposed: Therefore seeing we have the ministration, just as we have obtained mercy, we faint not.
first_reading.reason: 'this ministration' follows the Greek (ten diakonian tauten); the Latin shown has only 'habentes administrationem', with no 'hanc'.

second_reading.note: Article-less "administrationem" refers back to the ministry just described; "this" is a legitimate determiner choice, as in Douay.

withdrawn.latin: exhortetur corda vestra, et confirmet in omni opere et sermone bono.
withdrawn.english: comfort your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.

first_reading.proposed: encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.
first_reading.reason: "exhortetur" means exhort or encourage; "comfort" is the usual English for the Greek, not for this Latin verb (elsewhere "consolari" is the word for comfort).

second_reading.note: "exhortetur corda vestra": in Christian Latin "exhortari" covers hearten, console; "comfort your hearts" is within its range.

withdrawn.latin: Confitemini ergo alterutrum peccata vestra, et orate pro invicem ut salvemini: multum enim valet deprecatio justi assidua.
withdrawn.english: Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed; for the persistent prayer of a just person has great power.

first_reading.proposed: Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved; for the persistent prayer of a just person has great power.
first_reading.reason: "ut salvemini" is "that you may be saved"; "healed" follows the Greek verb, not the Clementine's distinctive "salvemini".

second_reading.note: "salvemini" in a context of sickness ("salvabit infirmum") can mean be made whole, healed, as "salvus fieri" does in the Gospels; within range.

withdrawn.latin: Quia et Christus semel pro peccatis nostris mortuus est, justus pro injustis, ut nos offerret Deo, mortificatus quidem carne, vivificatus autem spiritu.
withdrawn.english: For Christ also died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.

first_reading.proposed: For Christ also died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.
first_reading.reason: "ut nos offerret Deo" is "that he might offer us to God"; "bring us to God" renders the Greek verb, not "offerret".

second_reading.note: "offerret" (ob + ferre) properly means bring to, present; Douay itself renders "offerebant illi parvulos" as brought, so "bring us to God" is sound.
